name: Shock Meets a Heavy Bubble
question: What changes when the bubble is denser than the surrounding gas?
blurb: The same shock hitting a bubble three times denser than the gas around it. The shock slows inside the bubble and the vorticity has the opposite sense, so the interface deforms differently.
physics:
A shock wave moving through air meets a bubble of a different (here lighter) gas. Two things happen. First, the shock travels faster in the light gas, so it bends and focuses as it crosses the bubble. Second — and this is the key mechanism — the bubble's interface is a density gradient, while the shock is a pressure gradient, and where those two gradients are misaligned the equations generate vorticity. This is the baroclinic torque, ∝ ∇ρ × ∇p.

That deposited vorticity rolls the bubble up into a pair of counter-rotating vortices and stirs the two gases together. This shock-bubble interaction is the canonical model of the Richtmyer–Meshkov instability — the impulsive cousin of Rayleigh–Taylor — which controls mixing in supersonic combustion (scramjets) and is a central obstacle in inertial-confinement fusion, where it spoils the symmetry of the imploding fuel.

It is solved with exactly the same compressible Euler / HLLC machinery as the explosion; only the initial condition differs.
terms:
• U, F(U), ∂t U + ∇·F(U) = 0, γ — the compressible Euler conservation laws (see the Detonation exhibit)
• M_s — the shock Mach number you set; the post-shock density, pressure and velocity follow from the exact Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions, so a stronger shock means a hotter, faster, more compressed incoming flow
• ρ_bub/ρ_air — the bubble-to-air density ratio: below 1 the bubble is light (the shock speeds through and it rolls up fast), above 1 it is heavy (the shock focuses inside it); this ratio sets the sign and size of the baroclinic torque
• baroclinic vorticity generation, ∝ ∇ρ×∇p, is what rolls the bubble up
numerics: Same compressible finite-volume scheme (MUSCL + minmod, HLLC Riemann solver, SSP-RK2, γ = 1.4). One or two circular bubbles of a chosen density ratio sit in still air; the incoming flow is the exact Rankine–Hugoniot post-shock state for the Mach number you set, so shock strength and density contrast are both physical, tunable inputs.
ic: A planar incident shock travelling into still gas, set just upstream of a lighter (or heavier) gas bubble at rest; the twin-bubble variant seeds two.
bc: The incident shock is set as an initial condition (a post-shock slab); all domain edges are zero-gradient (weakly reflecting) outflow; the bubble is a density contrast, not a wall, so the shock passes through and deforms it.

experiment.name: Shock–bubble interaction
experiment.question: How does the density contrast alter the interface deformation?

params.name: target
params.label: Target
params.help: One gas bubble, or two stacked bubbles whose roll-ups interact.

params.name: mach
params.label: Shock Mach number
params.help: Strength of the incoming shock, M_s = (shock speed)/(sound speed). The post-shock state follows the exact Rankine–Hugoniot relations (see derived quantities).

params.name: densratio
params.label: Density ratio ρ_bubble/ρ_air
params.help: Bubble density ÷ ambient density. <1 = a light bubble (rolls up fast); >1 = a heavy bubble (the shock slows and focuses inside it).

params.name: bubble
params.label: Bubble size
params.help: Bubble radius as a fraction of the domain height.

params.name: resolution
params.label: Resolution
params.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

params.name: duration
params.label: Duration (×)
params.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
